newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks slide again on Liggett plan.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks slide again on Liggett plan.

text.p: Tobacco stocks were sharply lower in early trade amid reports that Brooke Group Ltd unit Liggett Group Inc would expand its litigation settlement plan with plaintiffs in tobacco suits to free more potentially damning information.

On the New York Stock Exchange, Philip Morris Cos Inc shares were down five at 117. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, parent company of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, saw its stock drop one, while Loews Corp was off 2-1/4.
On the American Stock Exchange, the newly christened Tobacco Index was down 8.15 at 282.30.
Liggett Group is said to be readying the announcement of a broader version of the settlement package it struck one year ago with potential plaintiffs, sources told Reuters Wednesday.
The accord would be expanded to include the Medicaid suits filed by 22 states in their effort to recoup the cost of smoking-related illnesses.
Liggett's previous settlement package, an unprecedented move at the time that rocked Wall Street, concentrated on suits filed by plaintiffs outside the Medicaid actions.

The new settlement would purportedly include the release of more documents about what tobacco companies knew with regard to the dangers of smoking, and warning labels on Liggett-brand cigarettes that admit cigarettes are addictive and carcinogenic.
Published reports said the deal would also include permission for former Liggett employees to come forward with any information they have about the company or the industry.
Lawyers close to the talks said the talks have been ongoing but no final deal is imminent.
Brooke Group shares were up 1/2 at 4-3/4.

Tobacco stocks have been repeatedly pressured over the past few weeks from news and rumors that grow increasingly ominous, despite assertions from analysts that the developments pose no added threats to the tobacco industry.
"It's an old settlement and it's not worth the paper it's written on," said Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Gary Black.
"You would think (this) time around investors would learn," Black said.
